title: Brute Force: Credential Stuffing
summary:
Credential stuffing is an automated credential access technique in which the adversary replays username and password pairs obtained from a breach of one service against authentication endpoints of other services, exploiting the fact that people reuse passwords across systems. Because each attempt uses a valid credential for some unrelated site, failure rates are low enough that modest volumes of traffic produce a meaningful number of successful logins, and per-account lockout counters are rarely triggered since each account typically sees one attempt. Attacks are usually executed from distributed residential proxy networks or botnets so that source reputation and address-based throttling do not stop the campaign.

Artefacts appear in authentication and web telemetry. Identity provider or application logs show a large number of logins from many distinct addresses that share a narrow fingerprint: identical client or user agent strings, identical header ordering, uniform inter-request timing, and no preceding session or page views. The ratio of successful to failed logins is often unusually high compared with normal user behaviour, and the first action after a successful login frequently differs from that account's historical pattern, such as immediately creating access tokens, changing registered authentication methods, or reading mailbox rules. Account recovery and password reset events may cluster afterwards if the legitimate user is displaced.

Benign lookalikes include shared network address translation egress, corporate proxy pools, and users travelling. What separates stuffing is the breadth of accounts touched, the uniformity of the client fingerprint, the absence of normal session establishment, and the correlation of the username set with a known third-party breach. Detection therefore depends on joining authentication outcomes with network-level fingerprinting rather than on any single log source.
objectives: Explain how password reuse and third-party breach data make stuffing viable, and why per-account lockout does not stop it.
Identify the client fingerprint characteristics that distinguish automated replay from genuine interactive login.
Correlate successful authentications with post-login behaviour to determine whether an account was actually taken over.
Analyse source address distribution and proxy patterns to differentiate stuffing infrastructure from corporate egress.
Prioritise accounts for forced reset and session revocation based on observed post-authentication activity.
Map credential stuffing to ATT&CK and describe the controls that reduce impact when passwords are already compromised.
